results.key_finding: The 2024 revision adds the optic nerve as a fifth region and accepts the kFLC index as an alternative to oligoclonal bands. Lesions in four or five regions establish dissemination in space without a separate test of dissemination in time; with two or three regions, dissemination in time, positive CSF or the central vein sign is needed.
results.title: Diagnosis of multiple sclerosis: 2024 revisions of the McDonald criteria

output.summary: Current guidelines recommend early initiation of disease-modifying therapy in patients with relapsing-remitting MS. First-line options include moderate-efficacy therapies (dimethyl fumarate, teriflunomide, glatiramer acetate, interferons) or higher-efficacy therapies (natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) depending on disease activity and prognostic factors. The 2024 revision of the McDonald criteria adds the optic nerve region and the kFLC index as diagnostic evidence.

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Thompson is a 28-year-old right-handed veterinary technician who presents to the neurology service after being referred from urgent care for progressive bilateral lower extremity weakness and new-onset urinary urgency. Her symptoms began approximately three weeks ago with a sensation of heaviness in both legs that she initially attributed to overexertion from a weekend hiking trip. Over the following days, the heaviness progressed to noticeable weakness, particularly in the right leg, making it difficult for her to climb the stairs to her second-floor apartment without gripping the railing tightly. She also reports a band-like tightness around her lower abdomen that has been constant since about two weeks ago, which she describes as feeling like a belt cinched too tightly around her waist.

Approximately ten days ago, she developed urinary urgency, noting that she frequently feels the need to urinate with little warning and has had two episodes of near-incontinence. She denies frank urinary retention or bowel dysfunction. She also reports intermittent tingling and numbness in both feet, worse on the right, that has been gradually worsening over the past two weeks.

When questioned about prior neurological symptoms, Ms. Thompson recalls an episode approximately eighteen months ago where she experienced blurred vision in her left eye lasting about two weeks. She describes the vision as being like looking through a frosted window and notes that it was accompanied by mild pain behind the eye, particularly with eye movement. She was seen by an ophthalmologist who diagnosed possible retrobulbar optic neuritis and recommended follow-up, but she did not pursue further workup at the time as her vision improved spontaneously. She denies any other prior neurological symptoms, including seizures, limb weakness, speech difficulties, or swallowing problems. She has not had any recent infections, fevers, or vaccinations. Her general health has been otherwise good aside from the conditions listed in her past medical history.
